1Theories of Aging

Section 1 Introduction

The actual life span of any single individual is determined by a multitude of factors
including lifestyle, socioeconomic status, diet, environmental conditions, and genetic
endowments. The most dramatic effect of diet on lifespan is illustrated by the lifespan of
the queen bee, compared to the worker bee.  The queen bee can live as long as 6 years
whereas worker bees live from 3 to 6 months, yet both the queen bee and the worker bee
have the identical genetic makeup. The difference in lifespan is simply the result of
whether of not the insects were fed royal jelly during their larva stage, which increases
their lifespan by some twenty-fold.

As an organism ages, its chances of death increases, so that all individuals of a given
species are dead by some age, characteristic of that species. It is estimated that the
maximum lifespan for humans is between 90 – 120 years, although authentic reports of
an individual living to be 122 years has been recorded. Theories to explain the
mechanism of aging are divided into two main categories:

1. Developmentally-programmed aging

2. Damage accumulation aging

Programmed theories view aging as the result of genetic regulation (e.g. telomere
shortening, hormonal changes etc). For example, with each cell division the telomeres
(protein-DNA structures at the ends of the chromosomes in each cell) undergo
shortening. At a critical level of telomere shortening cells show accelerated aging and an
inability to keep dividing and a greater tendency to undergo cancerous changes as well as
a greater susceptibility to free radical damage.
Damage theories view aging as the result of accumulated errors, primarily from free
radicals. The two theories are complementary in that changes in gene expression that
occur with cellular aging permit damage to occur to somatic cells that do not occur (or
accumulate) in immortal cells such as germ cells (immature spermatozoa in the testes and
the immature egg cells in the ovaries). In other words, aging does not occur in the germ
cells, yet it clearly does so beginning sometime after fertilization. Thus, free radical aging
is only allowed to begin (as determined by some genetic programming) only after
fertilization has occurred. Evidence indicates that not only does free radical production
increase substantially as we age, but the free radicals produced are less well contained
and less efficiently mopped up by antioxidants, and their consequent damage is less
efficiently repaired

Section 2 Developmentally-Programmed Aging

2

A. Telomeres

The ends of chromosomes consist of specialized nucleoprotein structures called
telomeres. Telomeres are protein DNA structures present at the ends of chromosomes and
are essential for genetic stability and cell replication . With each cell division, telomeres
shorten until they reach a certain critical length, which causes cells to undergo senescence
(cell cycle arrest).
Human telomeres function as a protective structure capping both ends of the
chromosome. Uncapped chromosome ends are at risk of degradation, recombination, or
fusion by cellular DNA repair systems, resulting in genetic information becoming lost,
rearranged, or unstable. Telomeres have been shown to protect the ends of chromosomes
from damage (free radicals) allowing for more complete replication of the chromosome,
controlling gene expression and aiding in the organization of the chromosome. At cell
replication, telomeres cannot be completely replicated. They are gradually shortened, and
when the telomeres reach a critical threshold, cell replication is arrested in what is called
"replicative senescence. Telomere length serves as an intrinsic biological clock regulating
the life span of the cell, in which a finite number of cell replications can occur, upon
which the cell undergoes replicative senescence.
To illustrate this point the human fibroblasts from young persons have long telomeres,
whereas older individuals have shorter telomeres. Similarly, patients with premature
aging syndrome (eg, Werner's syndrome and Hutchinson-Gilford's syndrome) have
shorter telomeres as compared with healthy individuals of the same age.   Thus, telomeres
limit the capacity of a cell to replicate, by inducing senescence as a sort of tumor-
suppressing mechanism. As discussed, with successive cell divisions, telomeres are
gradually shortened. When they reach a critical length, the induction of senescence is
associated with the activation of a number of pathways. As a consequence, cell growth is
arrested and apoptosis (programmed cell death) occurs. However, during malignant
transformation many cancer cells develop immortality by re-establishing telomere length
via the secretion of telomerase enzyme.
Of clinical and diagnostic significance, with respect determining biological age of an
individual, is the discovery that genetic determination of the regulation of telomere length
is tissue-independent. Results indicate that telomere length measurement in easily
accessible tissues such as blood cells could serve as a surrogate parameter for the relative
telomere length in other tissues.

Long-lived species (humans) have cells with a far greater division potential that those of
short-lived species like mice (humans live 5X longer than cats, who live 5X longer than
mice, who live 25X longer than fruit flies)

3Note that older people's cells in culture putter out much faster than those of younger
people. Cells of a fetus (in culture) divide quickly until they too, eventually slow down
and putter out.
At conception, telomere length is about 10,000 base pairs (compared to 130,000 base
pairs for entire chromosome). At birth telomere length is about 5,000 base pairs
Telomerase Enzyme
Telomere length is usually maintained by a ribonucleoprotein called telomerase, which
adds new DNA ends to chromosomes. This enzyme consists of a strand of RNA, called
hTR (or hTerc), and a catalytic protein component, called hTERT. During human
development, telomerase activity is detected in almost all tissues, while it is repressed in
most normal adult human somatic tissues. In adults, telomerase is still expressed in the
germline and in stem cells of renewable tissues such as bone marrow, skin, and the
gastrointestinal tract.
Telomerase activity is almost absent in somatic cells, but it is detected in embryonic stem
cells and in the vast majority of tumor cells. Tumor cells, in fact, may contain short and
stable telomeres that confer immortality to the cancer cells, which are thus able to
replicate indefinitely. The deregulation of telomeres thus plays an important role in the
relationship between premature aging syndrome and cancer

An Historical Perspective Of Telomere and Telomerase Research
In the early 1930s, Hermann J. Muller and Barbara McClintock described the telomere
(from the Greek word "telos," meaning end, and "meros," meaning part) as a protective
structure at the terminal end of the chromosome. When this structure is absent, end-to-
end fusion of the chromosome may occur, with ensuing cell death.
In the 1960s, Leonard Hayflick described a biological view of aging. He found that
human diploid cells proliferate a limited number of times in a cell culture. The "Hayflick
limit" is the maximal number of divisions that a cell can achieve in vitro. When cells
reach this limit, they undergo morphologic and biochemical changes that eventually lead
to arrest of cell proliferation, a process called "cell senescence". Hayflick noted that
human fibroblasts could replicate a total of 50 times in culture, before no further cell
division could occur. Near the final cell divisions, cells age more rapidly, look older, are
larger and accumulate lipofuscin pigment and other debris.
In the 1970s, James D. Watson described what he called "end-replication problems."
During DNA replication, DNA-dependent DNA polymerase does not completely

4replicate the extreme 5' terminal end of the chromosome, leaving a small region of
telomere uncopied, thus shortening the telomere with each cell division.
In the 1970s, Olovnikov connected cell senescence with end-replication problems in his
"Theory of Marginotomy," in which telomere shortening was proposed as an intrinsic
clocklike mechanism of aging that tracks the number of cell divisions before the arrest of
cell growth or replicative senescence sets in. Greider and colleagues, in 1988,
corroborated this theory when they observed a progressive loss in telomere length in
dividing cells cultured in vitro.
In 1978, Elizabeth Blackburn found that the molecular structure of telomeres in
Tetrahymena pyriformis  contains long repeating units rich in thymine (T) and guanine
(G) residues. In 1984, she and her colleagues isolated telomerase, the enzyme responsible
for the maintenance and elongation of telomere length. In 1989, Gregg reported the
existence of telomerase activity in human cancer cell lines, which was thought to
contribute to the immortality of tumor cells. At about the same time, Greider and
associates found that telomerase was nearly always absent in normal somatic cells.
In the 1990s, Shay and Harley detected telomerase in 90 of 101 human tumor cell
samples (from 12 different tumor types), but found no activity in 50 normal somatic cell
samples (from 4 different tissue types). Since then, more than 2600 human tumor samples
have been examined and telomerase activity detected in about 90% of all tumor cells. The
obvious implication is that telomerase may play a major role in the pathogenesis of
cancer.
Because of their role in physiologic aging, cancer pathogenesis, and premature aging
syndromes (eg, progeria), telomeres and telomerase are currently under intensive
investigation.

Cancer and Telomerase Expression

Stem cells express telomerase to maintain telomere length throughout their life cycle.
Many cancer cells have also been shown to express active telomerase. This might be a
mechanism for their ability to avoid senescence and become immortal. About 90% of
cancer cells contain short telomeres and high levels of telomerase activity. Alan Meeker,
of the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Baltimore, Maryland, has been
investigating whether telomere shortening is actually a causative factor in tumorigenesis,
or if it is simply a result of continuous cancer cell proliferation. Extensive research has
led Meeker to conclude that telomere shortening is a prevalent feature of human
premalignant epithelial cells. This supports the hypothesis that telomere shortening is an
early event in human tumor development, and that such shortening could contribute to the
chromosome mutagenesis and instability that are required for tumor progression. For
example, 75% of oral carcinomas, 80% of lung cancers, 84% of prostate cancers, 85% of
liver cancers, 93% of breast cancers, 94% of neuroblastomas, 95% of colorectal cancers,

5and 98% of bladder cancers have detectable telomerase activity. It remains to be
determined whether telomerase may represent a sensitive biomarker for diagnosis, early
detection, and prognosis of cancer. Since telomerase activity appears necessary for the
sustained proliferation of most cancer cells, anticancer agents based on telomerase
inhibition might provide an effective therapy.

Nutrition Can Speed Up Or Slow Down The Rate Of Cell Replication

Cellular and tissue aging, as well as increased risk of cancer are clearly related to the
shortening of telomeres with each cell division. Thus, any strategy that slows the rate of
cell division prolongs the time in which an organism (including humans) can enjoy the
benefits of healthier, more functional cells in all tissues and organs of the body, lower
risk of developing cancer, and in effect, slow the aging process. Certain nutritional
factors have been shown to either speed up or slow down the rate of cell division. Factors
that speed up the rate of cell division, and thus, are associated with more rapid aging, and
increased risk of cancer include:

1. A high animal fat diet - High levels of arachidonic acid give rise to the
formation of prostaglandin series 2 hormones, which increase the rate of cellular
replication throughout the body. The consumption of animal fat also increases the
secretion of bile acids into the intestinal tract from the gallbladder and liver. Bile acids
are readily converted by gut bacteria into secondary sterols, such as lithocholic acid and
deoxycholic acid. These secondary sterols are known to increase the cell division rate of
colonic epithelial cells and are associated with increased risk of colon cancer via this
action.

2. Alcohol - Alcohol speeds up the rate of cell division, generates free radicals
and acts as a co-carcinogen by enhancing the uptake of other carcinogens at the cellular
level.

3.Obesity - Overweight subjects convert more androstenedione into estrone
hormone within their fat tissue as a consequence of having larger fat cells. Estrone
hormone increases cellular replication of breast and other female reproductive tissues and
is strongly associated with increased breast cancer risk in postmenopausal women.
Overweight postmenopausal women have a three times greater-risk of breast cancer than
their leaner age-matched counterparts. Hormone replacement therapy increases risk of
breast cancer in much the same way. In men, higher estrone levels inhibit the breakdown
of dihydrotestosterone in the prostate gland. Dihydrotestosterone increases prostate cell
division rates and is strongly associated with prostate enlargement and prostate cancer.
Due largely to the consequence of creating insulin resistance, being overweight also
inhibits the secretion of sex hormone binding globulin from the liver, which in turn,
allows more estrogen and testosterone to circulate unbound to this important protein
carrier, which allows these hormones to exert stronger physiological effects on
reproductive tissue, speeding up of cell division rates with an associated increased risk of
reproductive cancers.

6Factors that slow down the rate of cell division and are thus, associated with a slowing of
biological aging and reduced risk of cancer include:

1. Omega-3 fats – Omega-3 fats from fish, fish oil and flaxseed oil give rise to
prostaglandin series-3, which slows cell division rates throughout the body.

2. Vitamin D – Stimulation of vitamin D receptors slows the rate of cell division.
Higher circulating levels of vitamin D are associated with a decreased risk of colon,
breast and prostate cancers. Calcium appears to work synergistically with vitamin D in
regards to slowing the replication rate of colonic epithelium and thereby, reducing risk of
colon cancer.

3. Vitamin A – Vitamin slows the rate of cell division and allows cells to fully
mature (differentiate) in a highly regulated fashion, both effects of which are associated
with reduced cancer risk

4. Nutrients That Inhibit The Synthesis Of Estrone Hormone In Fat Cells – As
mentioned above, over secretion of estrone hormone from fat cells directly or indirectly
speeds replication of breast, prostate and other reproductive tissues. Certain nutrients can
block the aromatase enzyme responsible for the conversion of androstenedione into
estrone hormone and thus, lower the circulating levels of this hormone. These protective
agents include soy isoflavones (genistein and diadzein), the indole-3- carbinol from
cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, bok choy) and
the phytoestrogens (enterolactone and enterodiol) produced by the gut bacteria upon
ingestion of flaxseed powder.

5. Bioactive Agents That Inhibit The Conversion Of Testosterone To
Dihydrotestosterone In The Male Prostate Gland – A build up of dihydrotestosterone in
the male prostate gland causes more rapid cellular replication leading to prostate
enlargement and possibly increased risk of prostate cancer. Soy isoflavones (especially
genistein), zinc, the bioactive agents in saw palmetto, and beta-sitosterol
supplementation, have all been shown to inhibit the 5-alpha Reductase enzyme that
converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, helping to slow prostate cell division rates.

Summary
Somatic cells are programmed to undergo only a limited number of cell divisions, after
which they enter a state called senescence. This is most readily apparent in vitro, where
cultured primary cells reach the end of their programmed lifespan, enlarge, and
permanently cease to divide.
During our lifetime, as liver cells, kidney cells and the cells of other organs use up their
maximum number of cell divisions and enter a state of senescence, fewer and fewer
functional cells remain within any given organ as we age. As such, there is an age-related
decline in functional capacity that affects most of the organ systems in the body due to

7the fact that each organ will possess a fewer number of functional cells as time goes by,
as individual cells reach their maximum replication potential. Thus, the ability of the
kidneys to filter toxins from the blood becomes less efficient over time, as does the
ability of the liver to detoxify blood toxins and the ability of the pancreas to secrete
optimal levels of digestive enzymes etc. In short, much of the functional decline in the
performance of the body's organ systems (which can lead to organ failure and death in
the case of liver and/or kidney failure), is related to a loss of functional cells as the body
ages. Therefore, any dietary or supplementation strategy that slows the rate of cell
division of somatic cells, in theory, slows aging of internal organs and the body as a
whole, and provides a longer period within one's lifespan in which these organs can
remain more highly functional.
Primary cells that are driven to proliferate by oncogenic transformation bypass
senescence and enter crisis, or massive cell death, as they approach the end of their
lifespan. The small number of cells that survive crisis are capable of an infinite number of
cell divisions, essentially becoming immortal cell lines. These in vitro studies have
provided a model to study the biological clock of normal somatic cells, one of the most
potent safeguards against malignant transformation and one that must be overcome by all
cancer cells destined to grow past their prescribed lifespan.
The cellular biological clock is linked to telomeres, the ends of chromosomes that are
necessary to maintain chromosomal integrity. Telomeres are composed of a stretch of
repeated nucleotides. Because DNA polymerase fails to copy the extreme ends of
chromosomes telomeres shrink with every cell division. Cellular senescence is well
correlated with the shortening of telomeres to less than the size required to maintain the
integrity of chromosomes. In contrast to somatic cells that have a finite lifespan, germ
cells and hematopoietic stem cells preserve the length of their telomeres with an enzyme
called telomerase. A ribonucleoprotein with reverse transcriptase activity, telomerase
uses an RNA template to add the appropriate nucleotide repeats to the ends of telomeres,
thus matching the progressive shortening that accompanies cell division. This physiologic
mechanism for circumventing senescence has been adapted by human tumors, most of
which express high levels of telomerase.

Stress Also Decreases Telomere Length and Speeds Cellular Aging
Chronic psychological stress is associated with accelerated telomere shortening and lower
telomerase activity in leukocytes, which may explain how stress may ultimately lead to
premature aging, according to a report in the Proceedings of the National Academy of
Sciences. A recent study on the relationship between stress and aging, included a cohort
of 39 healthy, premenopausal women who were primary care givers for a child with a
chronic illness. Control subjects were 19 age-matched mothers of healthy children.Stress
was measured with a standardized 10-item questionnaire in which the women reported
their perceived level of stress over the past month. Objective stress was determined using
the number of years since a child's diagnosis. Mean telomere length and telomerase

8activity were measured in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Oxidative stress was
assayed in samples of serum and urine. Within the care giving group, an increased
number of years as a caregiver was associated with shorter telomere length, lower activity
of telomerase, and greater oxidative stress. The same relationship was observed between
subjective stress and the markers of cellular aging. In the 14 women who comprised the
highest quartiles of perceived stress scores, telomeres averaged 3,110 base-pairs in
length, while the 14 in the lowest-stress quartile averaged 3,660 base pairs.
Of interest is the fact that during adulthood, telomere shortening averages 31 to 63 base
pairs per year, so the authors estimate that the 550-base pair shortening in the high-stress
group translates to 9 to 17 additional years of aging. These findings may have
implications for human health, since telomere shortening and reduced telomerase are
associated with premature death from cancer, cardiovascular and infectious disease.
While the number of years that mothers had been a care giver did matter, "not all
caregivers fell into the high-stress group," researchers noted. This implies that the ability
to better manage stress throughout one's lifetime appears to result in a slower reduction
in telomere length, and increased telomerase activity, which translates into slower
biological aging and reduced risk of certain degenerative diseases.

B. The NeuroEndocrine Clock
Programmed into the body's aging clock are what appears to be predetermined points in
the human lifecycle whereby hormonal changes are triggered, which permit the aging
process to advance more rapidly. At specific points in the lifecycle, which are highly
predictable, a distinct pattern of decline in hormone secretion occurs for melatonin,
growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor-1, DHEA, estrogen, progesterone and
thymosin (and other thymus gland hormones), with each hormone exhibiting its own
unique pattern of decline. The age-related altered patterns of hormone synthesis and
secretion are known to contribute to cellular aging of many target tissues and to many
clinical signs and symptoms associated with the aging process of the body as a whole.
Melatonin - melatonin is synthesized in the pineal gland from serotonin. Babies produce
increasing amounts of melatonin until they are about one year old. Then their nocturnal
melatonin levels (melatonin is primarily secreted at night to induce sleep) remain steady
until just before puberty, when they decline markedly, a trend that continues for the next
five years or so. The abrupt decline just before puberty appears to be part of the
neuroendocrine signal that triggers the onset of puberty. The onset of puberty is
associated with increased release of reproductive hormones and growth hormone. Animal
studies show that the administration of high levels of melatonin can inhibit reproduction.
In children, those who are late to enter puberty have been found to have higher levels of
melatonin than their peers, whereas individuals who enter puberty as early as three years
before their peers may produce only one-third as much melatonin as other children their
age.
Melatonin continues to decline from just before the onset of puberty through to age 70,
such that a person at age 9 or 10 years of age exhibits nighttime melatonin blood levels at
approximately 125 pg/ml compared to a 70 year old whose nighttime blood levels are
customarily 10-20 pg/ml. Melatonin is the hormone that induces deep levels of sleep,
helping the body to renew itself over night. This hormone is also important to regulate
and optimize immune function. The decline in melatonin secretion corresponds with the
time in our lifespan that is associated with the initial stages of shrinking of the thymus
gland, which is an important immune system gland. T-helper cells of the immune system
(a type of white blood cell) have been shown to have melatonin receptors. Upon

11stimulation by melatonin these immune cells release a number of signaling chemicals that
heighten the performance of many other immune cells and immune system activities.
Melatonin is also a powerful antioxidant, which protects the brain from free radical
damage (and other tissue sites as well). Melatonin has shown impressive anti-cancer and
tumor suppressive effects in animal studies and preliminary human trials. Animal studies
have shown that it can increase longevity of mice by up to 20% when provided in their
nightly drinking water, compared to mice not receiving melatonin during their lifespan.
The decline in melatonin secretion is considered to be an important hormonal factor in
the aging process.
Growth Hormone (GH)  – Growth hormone (somatotropin) is a single-chain peptide of
191 amino acids, and is the most abundant hormone in the body. It is produced by the
somatotroph cells in the anterior pituitary gland. Growth hormone (GH) declines in every

GH production rate is reduced by 50%, by the age of sixty. This means that at twenty
years old we make about 500 mcg per day, 200 mcg at forty years old and only 25 mcg at
80 years old. Once secreted by the anterior pituitary gland, growth hormone is extracted
from the blood stream by the liver where it stimulates the synthesis and release of insulin-
like growth factor-1, which produces the actual effects on our tissues that are attributed to
growth hormone. Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) has an anabolic effect on lean mass
and bone mass, and thus, speeds metabolism indirectly by encouraging lean mass
development. IGF-1 also strengthens immune function and appears to positively impact
libido. The age-related decline in GH and IGF-1 greatly contribute to the age-related loss
in lean mass (muscle catabolism) and bone loss, a gain in fat mass, and has been shown
to contribute to many other aspects of aging, which may include decreased energy,
thinning hair, increased wrinkles, sagging and loose skin, and frail nails
DHEA – DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) is produced by the adrenal glands upon
stimulation of ACTH (released by the pituitary gland), using cholesterol as a precursor.
DHEA is also produced in the ovaries and testis. DHEA is called the "the mother of all
steroids", and is the most abundant steroid hormone in the body. It is the parent
compound from which the body makes testosterone, estrogen, progesterone and
corticosterone. The body's internal clock alters the secretion rate of DHEA as we age,
which in turn, has far reaching effects on the aging process. The decline in DHEA
secretion parallels that of growth hormone. Blood levels of DHEA peak at about age 20
(men are usually in the range of 320-380 mcg/dl with women in the range of 200-250
mcg/dl), and begin to decline at a steady gradual rate after thirty. By age 75, many people
produce 75% less DHEA than they did at age 20. The indirect effects of DHEA decline
are usually first experienced between age 40 and 50. Because DHEA is the raw material
from which the body makes other steroid hormones,the drop off in DHEA production
impacts the synthesis of testosterone, estrogen and progesterone, which it turn, have
profound effects on the aging process of the body.
Testosterone  – The decline in DHEA production results in a decreased synthesis of
testosterone production by the testis and adrenal glands as men age. Studies indicate that

12there is a 1% decline in testosterone production each year between age 40 and 70, such
that a 70-year old man often shows a 30% reduction in blood testosterone levels
compared to a 40-year old man. Testosterone levels continue to drop off after age 70 as
well. The decline in testosterone production is strongly linked to many age-related
symptoms and complaints including reduced libido and sexual performance capabilities

contribute to low sex drive as well as age-related bone loss
Estrogen – Beginning at menopause there is a marked reduction in estrogen synthesis by

and ovulated egg cell that produces the majority of estrogen in the adult body of a
woman. The decline in estrogen secretion after age 50 encourages loss of calcium from
bone, an easier build of cholesterol in the blood stream (due to decreased LDL-

accelerated aging of the skin, hair and other tissues.
Conversely, in men, there is usually an increase in estrogen output by fat tissue as men

Section 3 Damage Accumulation Theories

A. Free Radicals, Antioxidants and Aging

Free radicals produced during normal metabolism cause damage to macromolecules. The
free radical theory of aging proposes that the organism is unable to repair all of the free
radical damage created and that, with time, un-repaired damage accumulates and puts the
organism at risk: in other words, free radicals provoke cellular aging and promote
biological changes within the organism that are associated with degenerative states and
increasing risk of death . In addition to exogenous free radicals such as cigarette smoke,
alcohol consumption, other pollutants and food-borne free radicals, many free radicals

14are reactive oxygen species that are byproducts of endogenous oxidation reactions. Free
radical damage has been implicated in the pathogenesis of several diseases.  According to
the free radical theory of aging, free radicals are involved in the production of changes in
cellular metabolism that lead to a time-dependent functional decline in all living beings.
Consequently, antioxidant and/or free radicals scavengers may retard the aging process.
Severe oxidative stress progressively leads to cell dysfunction and ultimately cell death.
Oxidative stress is defined as an imbalance between pro-oxidants and/or free radicals on
the one hand, and anti-oxidizing systems on the other. The oxygen required for living
may indirectly be responsible for negative effects; these deleterious effects are due to the
production of free radicals, which are toxic for the cells (superoxide anions, hydroxyl
radicals, peroxyl radicals, hydrogen peroxide, hydroperoxides and peroxinitrite anions).
Free radical attacks are responsible for cell damage and the targeted cells are represented
by the cell membranes, which are particularly rich in unsaturated fatty acids, sensitive to
oxidation reactions; DNA is also the target of severe attacks by these reactive oxygen
species (ROS). The cell's defense system is comprised of antioxidant enzymes and
antioxidant nutrients, which include such components as vitamins (E and C), enzymes
[superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione peroxidase (GPx) and others], and glutathione
reductase (GSH), capable of neutralizing peroxinitrite. The efficacy of this system is
dependent on the genome for the enzymatic defense systems, and on nutritional
antioxidants.  In addition to containing free radicals associated with aging,
epidemiological data suggest that antioxidants may have a beneficial effect on many age-
related diseases: atherosclerosis, cancer, some neurodegenerative and ocular diseases. For
instance, the post-secretory oxidation of LDL by oxygen free radicals results in the
unregulated uptake of cholesterol in arterial walls, which accelerates the atherosclerotic
process. Cumulative oxidative damage to DNA may be associated with the rise in cancer
risk that occurs with increasing age. Excess production of free radicals may also
contribute to tissue damage in rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel diseases
(including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis), cataracts, macular degeneration, and
neurodegenerative diseases and are strongly linked to the aging process . To fully
understand the relationship between oxygen, free radicals, antioxidants, and their effects
on aging and the disease process, a review of some evolutionary concepts and
physiological principles should prove helpful.

Humans Evolved As Oxygen Consumption Machines

Millions of years ago when the earth was formed, there was no free oxygen on the planet.
Then after a few millennia, one-celled creatures appeared that did not need oxygen to
survive. Instead, they used energy derived from the sun in a primitive version of
photosynthesis to draw carbon and nitrogen atoms directly from the atmosphere, which
became the raw materials they needed to sustain life. After a while more sophisticated
cells evolved that were able to use water as part of their photosynthesis process. A waste
product of this process was oxygen. Gradually these primeval life forms multiplied and
oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere. The process of photosynthesis converted an
atmosphere with virtually no free oxygen to an atmosphere that now is comprised of 21%
oxygen content. The original anaerobe creatures were now at a disadvantage, as they had
no protection against oxygen, which is highly toxic to an organism that has no

15antioxidant defenses (antioxidant enzymes, melatonin, alpha-lipoic acid and uric acid).
Natural selection now favored the appearance of organisms that could use oxygen in their
energy production pathway and at the same time protect themselves from the corrosive
effects of oxygen.
As such, more sophisticated oxygen-dependent organisms evolved (including humans)
that use oxygen in the conversion of macronutrients (carbohydrates, fat, protein, alcohol)
to ATP energy, which powers the biological machinery of the body. In human aerobic
metabolism, carbohydrates, protein, fat and alcohol are first converted to acetyl
Coenzyme A, which combines with oxaloacetate to enter the Krebs cycle, forming
citrate. During the many reactions within the Krebs cycle hydrogen atoms are removed
from the various intermediate compounds by niacin (NAD) and riboflavin (FAD). The
hydrogen atoms are then escorted to the electron transfer chain within the mitochondria
(the place where aerobic metabolism occurs) and the electrons from hydrogen are then
transferred from one cytochrome to the next until they reach the last cytochrome
(cytochrome oxidase). At that point 4 hydrogen electrons that have been shuttled down
the cytochrome chain react with one oxygen di-radical (two oxygen atoms attached
together written as O2 ) to form H2O (water). As the hydrogen electrons are passed from
one cytochrome to the next they are moving from higher to lower energy states. The
energy difference between the higher level of energy and the lower level of energy, as the
electrons move down the electron transfer chain, is given off as free energy and used to
re-couple ADP (adenosine monophosphate) with inorganic phosphate, to form ATP
(adenosine triphosphate). When enzymes split the outer most phosphate off from ATP, it
releases a large parcel of energy that is used to power the biological machinery of the
body (muscle contraction, energy dependent enzyme reactions etc.). At this point ATP
has lost a phosphate and is now in the form of ADP (adenosine diphosphate). As
hydrogen electrons continue to be shuttled down the cytochrome electron transfer chain,
ADP can once again be cycled back to ATP and the energy dependent reactions of the
body continue. Thus, to keep the cells of the body alive, the conversion of carbohydrate,
fat, protein (and when available, alcohol) to acetyl CoA, and the ultimate removal of
hydrogen atoms from Kreb cycle intermediates to be shuttled down the cytochrome
electron transfer chain to produce ATP, must continue at all times. If blood vessels
become clogged with atheroclerotic plaque (usually secondary to hypercholesterolemia)
then oxygen can no longer be delivered to the cells that are distal to the arterial blockage.
With no oxygen in the cell to receive the hydrogen electrons being shuttled down the
electron transfer chain, a backing up effect occurs in the electron transfer chain system,
whereby hydrogen electrons can no longer be shuttled from cytochrome to cytochrome.
The net result is that ATP can no longer be re-synthesized and cell death ensues due to an
energy shortage within the cell. This is classically what happens to myocardial cells
during a heart attack and in the brain during an ischemic stroke, cerebral vascular
insufficiency or a transient ischemic attack.
Also note that as we age the synthesis of coenzyme Q10 declines. Coenzyme Q10 is
required to shuttle hydrogen electrons from the first cytochrome to the second
cytochrome within the cytochrome electron transfer chain. A decline in coenzyme Q10
concentrations results in fewer hydrogen electrons being transferred down the through the
cytochrome system and the net result can be impaired ATP synthesis, which is linked to
the development of congestive heart failure, high blood pressure, aggravation of chronic

16stable angina and Parkinson's disease. This is why many anti-aging experts suggest
taking Coenzyme Q10 supplementation by age 40-50.

So Where Do The Oxygen Free Radicals Come From?

As noted above, hydrogen electrons (originally derived from macronutrients) are
continually shuttled from one cytochrome to the next within the electron transfer chain,
as means to release energy that re-couples ADP with inorganic phosphate to synthesize
ATP. This process is often referred to as oxidative phosphorylation. However, it is not a
foolproof system in that 2-5% of the hydrogen electrons leak out of the system (within
the cytochrome electron transfer chain). When they leak out of the system they become
very reactive with the oxygen di-radical (O2). Oxygen is missing two electrons in its
outer most orbital shells and is seeking to fill these outer most electron shells with the
missing electrons. When oxygen absorbs one hydrogen electron that has leaked out of the
system, it is then converted into a free radical known as the superoxide anion, which now
has one unpaired electron in its outer orbital shell. This is a highly reactive free radical
that will randomly steal an electron from a near by molecule (DNA, cell membrane
unsaturated fat, enzyme, etc.) in order to become electrically stable. However, the
molecule that has had and electron stolen away now has an unpaired electron of its own
and must, in turn, strips an electron away from another near by molecule, thereby
converting it into a free radical. And so free radical attack will continue within the cell
until the process is stopped by an antioxidant. Antioxidants can donate an electron to
stabilize a free radical without becoming converted into a free radical itself. (or more
correctly, via this process they quench more free radicals than they create, as some
antioxidants can become pro-oxidants under certain conditions, but in general,
antioxidants intercept free radicals and reduce free radical, oxidative stress to the cells of
the body).
In certain instances, the superoxide anion may absorb an additional hydrogen electron
that has leaked out of the system, which converts it into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
Hydrogen peroxide is known to travel throughout the cell and diffuse through the nuclear
membrane to reside in close proximity to the DNA of the cell. In the presence of a
transition metal (iron, copper, some heavy metals) hydrogen peroxide is easily converted
into hydroxy radicals (HO* plus *OH) when the transition metal donates an electron to
the reaction with hydrogen peroxide. In this instance the transitional metal becomes more
positively charged (e.g. divalent iron; ferrous iron, becomes trivalent iron; ferric iron).
The hydroxy radicals created in this instance are highly reactive oxygen free radicals that
are known to produce DNA damage and to damage many other cellular components.
The other oxygen free radical of importance is known as singlet oxygen, which is created
when the oxygen within our cells absorbs additional energy from X-rays, and/or ultra-
violet light (UV-light creates free radicals in the skin, and the lens and macula of the
eye).
Thus, oxygen is a double-edged sword in that we need oxygen within our cells to allow
the production of ATP to occur, and at the same time oxygen free radicals are
continuously being formed as by-products of a leaky, inefficient oxidative
phosphorylation system within the mitochondria of each cell, and the interaction of

17cellular oxygen with ultra-violet light and X-radiation energy. According to Russel
Reiter, a professor of neuroendocrinology at the University of Texas Health Science
Center at San Antonio, each cell is exposed to one trillion oxygen free radicals alone,
each day. Most of these free radicals are quenched by antioxidant enzymes, but not all of
them. Slowly over time the cumulative damage created by free radicals leads to the kind
of cellular damage associated with aging and degenerative diseases, including cancer.
Consistent with this process, the mitochondria theory of aging contends that free radical
damage to the mitochondria structure itself (the mitochondria is in close proximity to the
area where most of the oxygen free radicals are first created) damages the mitochondria
severely enough to reduce its capacity to generate ATP energy. The result is a power
shortage within the cell, which in turn leads to further cellular dysfunction, aging and
increased risk of cell death. Of interest to anti-aging practitioners is that coenzyme Q10,
alpha-lipoic acid, and Vitamin E have been shown to protect the mitochondrial
membrane and mitochondrial DNA, from free radical damage, by acting as antioxidants
in this area of the cell. This is a further reason to consider coenzyme Q10
supplementation by age 40 and lifelong supplementation with Vitamin E.
In terms of why some species age more slowly and live longer than others, some
available data indicate that the relation between oxidative stress and aging is due to the
presence of low rates of mitochondrial free radical production and low degrees of fatty
acid unsaturation of cellular membranes in the post-mitotic tissues of long-lived animals
in relation to those of short-lived ones. Recent research shows that long-lived animals
also have lower steady-state levels of oxidative damage in the mitochondrial DNA
(mtDNA) of post-mitotic cells than short-lived species. Studies also show that the flux of
free radical attack to mtDNA is higher in short- than in long-lived animals, and suggest
that this is a main determinant of the rate of accumulation of mtDNA mutations, and thus
the rate of aging.

A Quick Review of Oxygen Free Radicals And Antioxidants In The Aging Process
As stated above there are four common oxygen metabolites in biologic systems that are
free radicals: superoxide anion (O 2-), hydrogen peroxide (H 2O2), hydroxyl radical (OH
), and singlet oxygen (1O2). These free radicals can be generated via a number of
mechanisms, including normal physiologic processes and processes resulting from
external factors. For example, singlet oxygen is generated by photosensitization reactions
wherein a molecule absorbs light of a given wavelength, exciting the molecule. This
excited molecule transfers the increased energy to molecular oxygen, creating singlet
oxygen, which then can attack other cell components. It appears that the primary function
of carotenoids, an important class of antioxidants, is to scavenge free radicals,
particularly singlet oxygen produced by photosensitization.
A certain amount of oxidative function is necessary for proper health. For example,
oxidation processes are used by the body's immune systems to kill microorganisms.
Sometimes, however, the level of toxic reactive oxygen intermediates (ROI) overcomes
the antioxidant defenses of the host, resulting in an excess of free radicals and a state
called oxidative stress. These free radicals can induce local injury by reacting with lipids,

18proteins, and nucleic acids. The interaction of free radicals with cellular lipids leads to
membrane damage and the generation of lipid peroxide byproducts.
Cells contain a number of antioxidants that have various roles in protecting against free
radical reactions. The major water-soluble antioxidant metabolites are glutathione (GSH)
and vitamin C, which reside primarily in the cytoplasm and mitochondria. Many water-
soluble enzymes also catalyze these reactions. Glutathione peroxidase catalyzes the
reaction between GSH and hydrogen peroxide to form water and oxidized glutathione,
which is stable.
Vitamin E and the carotenoids are the principal lipid-soluble antioxidants. Vitamin E is
the major lipid-soluble antioxidant in cell membranes that can break the chain of lipid
peroxidation. Therefore, theoretically, it is the most important antioxidant in preventing
oxidation of these fatty acids. Vitamin E is recycled by a reaction with vitamin C.
Despite the actions of antioxidant nutrients, some oxidative damage will occur, and
accumulation of this damage throughout life is believed to be a major contributing factor
to aging and disease.

In addition to their importance to degenerative diseases and cellular aging, free radicals
also appear to be responsible for the increase in cross-linking between collagen fibers
within our body tissues as we age. One of the most common proteins found in the skin,
tendons, ligaments, bone, and cartilage is collagen. Very youthful collagen exhibits
widely spaced cross-linking between parallel collagen fibers (like rungs in ladder
connecting the two main legs together). It appears that free radicals are responsible for
the increased number of cross-links (increased number of rungs in the ladder) that occur
in our collagen as we age. The increased cross-linking causes the skin to shrink, and our
muscles, joints and tendons to become stiffer and less flexible and pliable, and reduces
the expansive capacity of our lungs, which contributes to the pulmonary functional
decline that accompanies aging. Thus, reduced free radical exposure and more superior
status of antioxidants status may also reduce the rate of collagen cross-linking, which
counters other important aspects of aging.

In the presence of elevated blood glucose levels, many of the body's proteins become
glycosylated (sugar coated by glucose or sorbitol). Virtually all proteins in the body that
are rich in the amino acid lysine can undergo glycosylation as a consequence of the
reaction of the epsilon amino group on lysine, with the aldose form of glucose, to form a
glycosylated protein. Proteins such as serum albumin and hemoglobin rapidly undergo
glycosylation when blood glucose levels are elevated. Glycosylated proteins are known to
clog blood vessels, damage internal organs and contribute to cataract formation. The
degree of protein glycosylation has been used as a marker for biological aging of specific
organs and loss of reserve function. The best evaluation of recent glycosylated protein
activity (previous 17-20 days) is measured by assessing fructosamine concentrations from
blood samples. A normal reading is in the about 2.06 mmol/l, and when corrected for

1Theories of Aging

Section 1 Introduction

The actual life span of any single individual is determined by a multitude of factors
including lifestyle, socioeconomic status, diet, environmental conditions, and genetic
endowments. The most dramatic effect of diet on lifespan is illustrated by the lifespan of
the queen bee, compared to the worker bee.  The queen bee can live as long as 6 years
whereas worker bees live from 3 to 6 months, yet both the queen bee and the worker bee
have the identical genetic makeup. The difference in lifespan is simply the result of
whether of not the insects were fed royal jelly during their larva stage, which increases
their lifespan by some twenty-fold.

As an organism ages, its chances of death increases, so that all individuals of a given
species are dead by some age, characteristic of that species. It is estimated that the
maximum lifespan for humans is between 90 – 120 years, although authentic reports of
an individual living to be 122 years has been recorded. Theories to explain the
mechanism of aging are divided into two main categories:

1. Developmentally-programmed aging

2. Damage accumulation aging

Programmed theories view aging as the result of genetic regulation (e.g. telomere
shortening, hormonal changes etc). For example, with each cell division the telomeres
(protein-DNA structures at the ends of the chromosomes in each cell) undergo
shortening. At a critical level of telomere shortening cells show accelerated aging and an
inability to keep dividing and a greater tendency to undergo cancerous changes as well as
a greater susceptibility to free radical damage.
Damage theories view aging as the result of accumulated errors, primarily from free
radicals. The two theories are complementary in that changes in gene expression that
occur with cellular aging permit damage to occur to somatic cells that do not occur (or
accumulate) in immortal cells such as germ cells (immature spermatozoa in the testes and
the immature egg cells in the ovaries). In other words, aging does not occur in the germ
cells, yet it clearly does so beginning sometime after fertilization. Thus, free radical aging
is only allowed to begin (as determined by some genetic programming) only after
fertilization has occurred. Evidence indicates that not only does free radical production
increase substantially as we age, but the free radicals produced are less well contained
and less efficiently mopped up by antioxidants, and their consequent damage is less
efficiently repaired

A. Telomeres

The ends of chromosomes consist of specialized nucleoprotein structures called
telomeres. Telomeres are protein DNA structures present at the ends of chromosomes and
are essential for genetic stability and cell replication . With each cell division, telomeres
shorten until they reach a certain critical length, which causes cells to undergo senescence
(cell cycle arrest).
Human telomeres function as a protective structure capping both ends of the
chromosome. Uncapped chromosome ends are at risk of degradation, recombination, or
fusion by cellular DNA repair systems, resulting in genetic information becoming lost,
rearranged, or unstable. Telomeres have been shown to protect the ends of chromosomes
from damage (free radicals) allowing for more complete replication of the chromosome,
controlling gene expression and aiding in the organization of the chromosome. At cell
replication, telomeres cannot be completely replicated. They are gradually shortened, and
when the telomeres reach a critical threshold, cell replication is arrested in what is called
"replicative senescence. Telomere length serves as an intrinsic biological clock regulating
the life span of the cell, in which a finite number of cell replications can occur, upon
which the cell undergoes replicative senescence.
To illustrate this point the human fibroblasts from young persons have long telomeres,
whereas older individuals have shorter telomeres. Similarly, patients with premature
aging syndrome (eg, Werner's syndrome and Hutchinson-Gilford's syndrome) have
shorter telomeres as compared with healthy individuals of the same age.   Thus, telomeres
limit the capacity of a cell to replicate, by inducing senescence as a sort of tumor-
suppressing mechanism. As discussed, with successive cell divisions, telomeres are
gradually shortened. When they reach a critical length, the induction of senescence is
associated with the activation of a number of pathways. As a consequence, cell growth is
arrested and apoptosis (programmed cell death) occurs. However, during malignant
transformation many cancer cells develop immortality by re-establishing telomere length
via the secretion of telomerase enzyme.
Of clinical and diagnostic significance, with respect determining biological age of an
individual, is the discovery that genetic determination of the regulation of telomere length
is tissue-independent. Results indicate that telomere length measurement in easily
accessible tissues such as blood cells could serve as a surrogate parameter for the relative
telomere length in other tissues.

Long-lived species (humans) have cells with a far greater division potential that those of
short-lived species like mice (humans live 5X longer than cats, who live 5X longer than
mice, who live 25X longer than fruit flies)

Telomerase Enzyme
Telomere length is usually maintained by a ribonucleoprotein called telomerase, which
adds new DNA ends to chromosomes. This enzyme consists of a strand of RNA, called
hTR (or hTerc), and a catalytic protein component, called hTERT. During human
development, telomerase activity is detected in almost all tissues, while it is repressed in
most normal adult human somatic tissues. In adults, telomerase is still expressed in the
germline and in stem cells of renewable tissues such as bone marrow, skin, and the
gastrointestinal tract.
Telomerase activity is almost absent in somatic cells, but it is detected in embryonic stem
cells and in the vast majority of tumor cells. Tumor cells, in fact, may contain short and
stable telomeres that confer immortality to the cancer cells, which are thus able to
replicate indefinitely. The deregulation of telomeres thus plays an important role in the
relationship between premature aging syndrome and cancer

An Historical Perspective Of Telomere and Telomerase Research
In the early 1930s, Hermann J. Muller and Barbara McClintock described the telomere
(from the Greek word "telos," meaning end, and "meros," meaning part) as a protective
structure at the terminal end of the chromosome. When this structure is absent, end-to-
end fusion of the chromosome may occur, with ensuing cell death.
In the 1960s, Leonard Hayflick described a biological view of aging. He found that
human diploid cells proliferate a limited number of times in a cell culture. The "Hayflick
limit" is the maximal number of divisions that a cell can achieve in vitro. When cells
reach this limit, they undergo morphologic and biochemical changes that eventually lead
to arrest of cell proliferation, a process called "cell senescence". Hayflick noted that
human fibroblasts could replicate a total of 50 times in culture, before no further cell
division could occur. Near the final cell divisions, cells age more rapidly, look older, are
larger and accumulate lipofuscin pigment and other debris.
In the 1970s, James D. Watson described what he called "end-replication problems."
During DNA replication, DNA-dependent DNA polymerase does not completely

--- Page Break ---

4replicate the extreme 5' terminal end of the chromosome, leaving a small region of
telomere uncopied, thus shortening the telomere with each cell division.
In the 1970s, Olovnikov connected cell senescence with end-replication problems in his
"Theory of Marginotomy," in which telomere shortening was proposed as an intrinsic
clocklike mechanism of aging that tracks the number of cell divisions before the arrest of
cell growth or replicative senescence sets in. Greider and colleagues, in 1988,
corroborated this theory when they observed a progressive loss in telomere length in
dividing cells cultured in vitro.
In 1978, Elizabeth Blackburn found that the molecular structure of telomeres in
Tetrahymena pyriformis  contains long repeating units rich in thymine (T) and guanine
(G) residues. In 1984, she and her colleagues isolated telomerase, the enzyme responsible
for the maintenance and elongation of telomere length. In 1989, Gregg reported the
existence of telomerase activity in human cancer cell lines, which was thought to
contribute to the immortality of tumor cells. At about the same time, Greider and
associates found that telomerase was nearly always absent in normal somatic cells.
In the 1990s, Shay and Harley detected telomerase in 90 of 101 human tumor cell
samples (from 12 different tumor types), but found no activity in 50 normal somatic cell
samples (from 4 different tissue types). Since then, more than 2600 human tumor samples
have been examined and telomerase activity detected in about 90% of all tumor cells. The
obvious implication is that telomerase may play a major role in the pathogenesis of
cancer.
Because of their role in physiologic aging, cancer pathogenesis, and premature aging
syndromes (eg, progeria), telomeres and telomerase are currently under intensive
investigation.

Cancer and Telomerase Expression

Stem cells express telomerase to maintain telomere length throughout their life cycle.
Many cancer cells have also been shown to express active telomerase. This might be a
mechanism for their ability to avoid senescence and become immortal. About 90% of
cancer cells contain short telomeres and high levels of telomerase activity. Alan Meeker,
of the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Baltimore, Maryland, has been
investigating whether telomere shortening is actually a causative factor in tumorigenesis,
or if it is simply a result of continuous cancer cell proliferation. Extensive research has
led Meeker to conclude that telomere shortening is a prevalent feature of human
premalignant epithelial cells. This supports the hypothesis that telomere shortening is an
early event in human tumor development, and that such shortening could contribute to the
chromosome mutagenesis and instability that are required for tumor progression. For
example, 75% of oral carcinomas, 80% of lung cancers, 84% of prostate cancers, 85% of
liver cancers, 93% of breast cancers, 94% of neuroblastomas, 95% of colorectal cancers,

--- Page Break ---

5and 98% of bladder cancers have detectable telomerase activity. It remains to be
determined whether telomerase may represent a sensitive biomarker for diagnosis, early
detection, and prognosis of cancer. Since telomerase activity appears necessary for the
sustained proliferation of most cancer cells, anticancer agents based on telomerase
inhibition might provide an effective therapy.

Nutrition Can Speed Up Or Slow Down The Rate Of Cell Replication

Cellular and tissue aging, as well as increased risk of cancer are clearly related to the
shortening of telomeres with each cell division. Thus, any strategy that slows the rate of
cell division prolongs the time in which an organism (including humans) can enjoy the
benefits of healthier, more functional cells in all tissues and organs of the body, lower
risk of developing cancer, and in effect, slow the aging process. Certain nutritional
factors have been shown to either speed up or slow down the rate of cell division. Factors
that speed up the rate of cell division, and thus, are associated with more rapid aging, and
increased risk of cancer include:

1. A high animal fat diet - High levels of arachidonic acid give rise to the
formation of prostaglandin series 2 hormones, which increase the rate of cellular
replication throughout the body. The consumption of animal fat also increases the
secretion of bile acids into the intestinal tract from the gallbladder and liver. Bile acids
are readily converted by gut bacteria into secondary sterols, such as lithocholic acid and
deoxycholic acid. These secondary sterols are known to increase the cell division rate of
colonic epithelial cells and are associated with increased risk of colon cancer via this
action.

2. Alcohol - Alcohol speeds up the rate of cell division, generates free radicals
and acts as a co-carcinogen by enhancing the uptake of other carcinogens at the cellular
level.

3.Obesity - Overweight subjects convert more androstenedione into estrone
hormone within their fat tissue as a consequence of having larger fat cells. Estrone
hormone increases cellular replication of breast and other female reproductive tissues and
is strongly associated with increased breast cancer risk in postmenopausal women.
Overweight postmenopausal women have a three times greater-risk of breast cancer than
their leaner age-matched counterparts. Hormone replacement therapy increases risk of
breast cancer in much the same way. In men, higher estrone levels inhibit the breakdown
of dihydrotestosterone in the prostate gland. Dihydrotestosterone increases prostate cell
division rates and is strongly associated with prostate enlargement and prostate cancer.
Due largely to the consequence of creating insulin resistance, being overweight also
inhibits the secretion of sex hormone binding globulin from the liver, which in turn,
allows more estrogen and testosterone to circulate unbound to this important protein
carrier, which allows these hormones to exert stronger physiological effects on
reproductive tissue, speeding up of cell division rates with an associated increased risk of
reproductive cancers.

biological aging and reduced risk of cancer include:

1. Omega-3 fats – Omega-3 fats from fish, fish oil and flaxseed oil give rise to
prostaglandin series-3, which slows cell division rates throughout the body.

2. Vitamin D – Stimulation of vitamin D receptors slows the rate of cell division.
Higher circulating levels of vitamin D are associated with a decreased risk of colon,
breast and prostate cancers. Calcium appears to work synergistically with vitamin D in
regards to slowing the replication rate of colonic epithelium and thereby, reducing risk of
colon cancer.

3. Vitamin A – Vitamin slows the rate of cell division and allows cells to fully
mature (differentiate) in a highly regulated fashion, both effects of which are associated
with reduced cancer risk

4. Nutrients That Inhibit The Synthesis Of Estrone Hormone In Fat Cells – As
mentioned above, over secretion of estrone hormone from fat cells directly or indirectly
speeds replication of breast, prostate and other reproductive tissues. Certain nutrients can
block the aromatase enzyme responsible for the conversion of androstenedione into
estrone hormone and thus, lower the circulating levels of this hormone. These protective
agents include soy isoflavones (genistein and diadzein), the indole-3- carbinol from
cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, bok choy) and
the phytoestrogens (enterolactone and enterodiol) produced by the gut bacteria upon
ingestion of flaxseed powder.

5. Bioactive Agents That Inhibit The Conversion Of Testosterone To
Dihydrotestosterone In The Male Prostate Gland – A build up of dihydrotestosterone in
the male prostate gland causes more rapid cellular replication leading to prostate
enlargement and possibly increased risk of prostate cancer. Soy isoflavones (especially
genistein), zinc, the bioactive agents in saw palmetto, and beta-sitosterol
supplementation, have all been shown to inhibit the 5-alpha Reductase enzyme that
converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, helping to slow prostate cell division rates.

Summary
Somatic cells are programmed to undergo only a limited number of cell divisions, after
which they enter a state called senescence. This is most readily apparent in vitro, where
cultured primary cells reach the end of their programmed lifespan, enlarge, and
permanently cease to divide.
During our lifetime, as liver cells, kidney cells and the cells of other organs use up their
maximum number of cell divisions and enter a state of senescence, fewer and fewer
functional cells remain within any given organ as we age. As such, there is an age-related
decline in functional capacity that affects most of the organ systems in the body due to

--- Page Break ---

7the fact that each organ will possess a fewer number of functional cells as time goes by,
as individual cells reach their maximum replication potential. Thus, the ability of the
kidneys to filter toxins from the blood becomes less efficient over time, as does the
ability of the liver to detoxify blood toxins and the ability of the pancreas to secrete
optimal levels of digestive enzymes etc. In short, much of the functional decline in the
performance of the body's organ systems (which can lead to organ failure and death in
the case of liver and/or kidney failure), is related to a loss of functional cells as the body
ages. Therefore, any dietary or supplementation strategy that slows the rate of cell
division of somatic cells, in theory, slows aging of internal organs and the body as a
whole, and provides a longer period within one's lifespan in which these organs can
remain more highly functional.
Primary cells that are driven to proliferate by oncogenic transformation bypass
senescence and enter crisis, or massive cell death, as they approach the end of their
lifespan. The small number of cells that survive crisis are capable of an infinite number of
cell divisions, essentially becoming immortal cell lines. These in vitro studies have
provided a model to study the biological clock of normal somatic cells, one of the most
potent safeguards against malignant transformation and one that must be overcome by all
cancer cells destined to grow past their prescribed lifespan.
The cellular biological clock is linked to telomeres, the ends of chromosomes that are
necessary to maintain chromosomal integrity. Telomeres are composed of a stretch of
repeated nucleotides. Because DNA polymerase fails to copy the extreme ends of
chromosomes telomeres shrink with every cell division. Cellular senescence is well
correlated with the shortening of telomeres to less than the size required to maintain the
integrity of chromosomes. In contrast to somatic cells that have a finite lifespan, germ
cells and hematopoietic stem cells preserve the length of their telomeres with an enzyme
called telomerase. A ribonucleoprotein with reverse transcriptase activity, telomerase
uses an RNA template to add the appropriate nucleotide repeats to the ends of telomeres,
thus matching the progressive shortening that accompanies cell division. This physiologic
mechanism for circumventing senescence has been adapted by human tumors, most of
which express high levels of telomerase.

Stress Also Decreases Telomere Length and Speeds Cellular Aging
Chronic psychological stress is associated with accelerated telomere shortening and lower
telomerase activity in leukocytes, which may explain how stress may ultimately lead to
premature aging, according to a report in the Proceedings of the National Academy of
Sciences. A recent study on the relationship between stress and aging, included a cohort
of 39 healthy, premenopausal women who were primary care givers for a child with a
chronic illness. Control subjects were 19 age-matched mothers of healthy children.Stress
was measured with a standardized 10-item questionnaire in which the women reported
their perceived level of stress over the past month. Objective stress was determined using
the number of years since a child's diagnosis. Mean telomere length and telomerase

--- Page Break ---

8activity were measured in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Oxidative stress was
assayed in samples of serum and urine. Within the care giving group, an increased
number of years as a caregiver was associated with shorter telomere length, lower activity
of telomerase, and greater oxidative stress. The same relationship was observed between
subjective stress and the markers of cellular aging. In the 14 women who comprised the
highest quartiles of perceived stress scores, telomeres averaged 3,110 base-pairs in
length, while the 14 in the lowest-stress quartile averaged 3,660 base pairs.
Of interest is the fact that during adulthood, telomere shortening averages 31 to 63 base
pairs per year, so the authors estimate that the 550-base pair shortening in the high-stress
group translates to 9 to 17 additional years of aging. These findings may have
implications for human health, since telomere shortening and reduced telomerase are
associated with premature death from cancer, cardiovascular and infectious disease.
While the number of years that mothers had been a care giver did matter, "not all
caregivers fell into the high-stress group," researchers noted. This implies that the ability
to better manage stress throughout one's lifetime appears to result in a slower reduction
in telomere length, and increased telomerase activity, which translates into slower
biological aging and reduced risk of certain degenerative diseases.

B. The NeuroEndocrine Clock
Programmed into the body's aging clock are what appears to be predetermined points in
the human lifecycle whereby hormonal changes are triggered, which permit the aging
process to advance more rapidly. At specific points in the lifecycle, which are highly
predictable, a distinct pattern of decline in hormone secretion occurs for melatonin,
growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor-1, DHEA, estrogen, progesterone and
thymosin (and other thymus gland hormones), with each hormone exhibiting its own
unique pattern of decline. The age-related altered patterns of hormone synthesis and
secretion are known to contribute to cellular aging of many target tissues and to many
clinical signs and symptoms associated with the aging process of the body as a whole.
Melatonin - melatonin is synthesized in the pineal gland from serotonin. Babies produce
increasing amounts of melatonin until they are about one year old. Then their nocturnal
melatonin levels (melatonin is primarily secreted at night to induce sleep) remain steady
until just before puberty, when they decline markedly, a trend that continues for the next
five years or so. The abrupt decline just before puberty appears to be part of the
neuroendocrine signal that triggers the onset of puberty. The onset of puberty is
associated with increased release of reproductive hormones and growth hormone. Animal
studies show that the administration of high levels of melatonin can inhibit reproduction.
In children, those who are late to enter puberty have been found to have higher levels of
melatonin than their peers, whereas individuals who enter puberty as early as three years
before their peers may produce only one-third as much melatonin as other children their
age.
Melatonin continues to decline from just before the onset of puberty through to age 70,
such that a person at age 9 or 10 years of age exhibits nighttime melatonin blood levels at
approximately 125 pg/ml compared to a 70 year old whose nighttime blood levels are
customarily 10-20 pg/ml. Melatonin is the hormone that induces deep levels of sleep,
helping the body to renew itself over night. This hormone is also important to regulate
and optimize immune function. The decline in melatonin secretion corresponds with the
time in our lifespan that is associated with the initial stages of shrinking of the thymus
gland, which is an important immune system gland. T-helper cells of the immune system
(a type of white blood cell) have been shown to have melatonin receptors. Upon

--- Page Break ---

11stimulation by melatonin these immune cells release a number of signaling chemicals that
heighten the performance of many other immune cells and immune system activities.
Melatonin is also a powerful antioxidant, which protects the brain from free radical
damage (and other tissue sites as well). Melatonin has shown impressive anti-cancer and
tumor suppressive effects in animal studies and preliminary human trials. Animal studies
have shown that it can increase longevity of mice by up to 20% when provided in their
nightly drinking water, compared to mice not receiving melatonin during their lifespan.
The decline in melatonin secretion is considered to be an important hormonal factor in
the aging process.

libido. The age-related decline in GH and IGF-1 greatly contribute to the age-related loss
in lean mass (muscle catabolism) and bone loss, a gain in fat mass, and has been shown

thinning hair, increased wrinkles, sagging and loose skin, and frail nails

profound effects on the aging process of the body.

Section 3 Damage Accumulation Theories

A. Free Radicals, Antioxidants and Aging

Free radicals produced during normal metabolism cause damage to macromolecules. The
free radical theory of aging proposes that the organism is unable to repair all of the free
radical damage created and that, with time, un-repaired damage accumulates and puts the
organism at risk: in other words, free radicals provoke cellular aging and promote
biological changes within the organism that are associated with degenerative states and
increasing risk of death . In addition to exogenous free radicals such as cigarette smoke,
alcohol consumption, other pollutants and food-borne free radicals, many free radicals

--- Page Break ---

14are reactive oxygen species that are byproducts of endogenous oxidation reactions. Free
radical damage has been implicated in the pathogenesis of several diseases.  According to
the free radical theory of aging, free radicals are involved in the production of changes in
cellular metabolism that lead to a time-dependent functional decline in all living beings.
Consequently, antioxidant and/or free radicals scavengers may retard the aging process.
Severe oxidative stress progressively leads to cell dysfunction and ultimately cell death.
Oxidative stress is defined as an imbalance between pro-oxidants and/or free radicals on
the one hand, and anti-oxidizing systems on the other. The oxygen required for living
may indirectly be responsible for negative effects; these deleterious effects are due to the
production of free radicals, which are toxic for the cells (superoxide anions, hydroxyl
radicals, peroxyl radicals, hydrogen peroxide, hydroperoxides and peroxinitrite anions).
Free radical attacks are responsible for cell damage and the targeted cells are represented
by the cell membranes, which are particularly rich in unsaturated fatty acids, sensitive to
oxidation reactions; DNA is also the target of severe attacks by these reactive oxygen
species (ROS). The cell's defense system is comprised of antioxidant enzymes and
antioxidant nutrients, which include such components as vitamins (E and C), enzymes
[superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione peroxidase (GPx) and others], and glutathione
reductase (GSH), capable of neutralizing peroxinitrite. The efficacy of this system is
dependent on the genome for the enzymatic defense systems, and on nutritional
antioxidants.  In addition to containing free radicals associated with aging,
epidemiological data suggest that antioxidants may have a beneficial effect on many age-
related diseases: atherosclerosis, cancer, some neurodegenerative and ocular diseases. For
instance, the post-secretory oxidation of LDL by oxygen free radicals results in the
unregulated uptake of cholesterol in arterial walls, which accelerates the atherosclerotic
process. Cumulative oxidative damage to DNA may be associated with the rise in cancer
risk that occurs with increasing age. Excess production of free radicals may also
contribute to tissue damage in rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel diseases
(including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis), cataracts, macular degeneration, and
neurodegenerative diseases and are strongly linked to the aging process . To fully
understand the relationship between oxygen, free radicals, antioxidants, and their effects
on aging and the disease process, a review of some evolutionary concepts and
physiological principles should prove helpful.

Humans Evolved As Oxygen Consumption Machines

Millions of years ago when the earth was formed, there was no free oxygen on the planet.
Then after a few millennia, one-celled creatures appeared that did not need oxygen to
survive. Instead, they used energy derived from the sun in a primitive version of
photosynthesis to draw carbon and nitrogen atoms directly from the atmosphere, which
became the raw materials they needed to sustain life. After a while more sophisticated
cells evolved that were able to use water as part of their photosynthesis process. A waste
product of this process was oxygen. Gradually these primeval life forms multiplied and
oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere. The process of photosynthesis converted an
atmosphere with virtually no free oxygen to an atmosphere that now is comprised of 21%
oxygen content. The original anaerobe creatures were now at a disadvantage, as they had
no protection against oxygen, which is highly toxic to an organism that has no
